bib.title: Training Verifiers to Solve Math Word Problems

read.skipped: Appendix D example solutions are images (no text).

question: Can training a verifier to rank sampled solutions improve multi-step grade-school math performance beyond fine-tuning a generator, and how does it scale with data?
hypothesis: Verification is easier than generation and gives optionality, so verifiers should scale better with data and model size than a fine-tuning baseline.
contributions: A curated dataset of 8.5K grade school math questions and natural language solutions (GSM8K).
Verifiers give about the same boost as a 30x model size increase over finetuning, and scale better with data.
Dropout acts as a strong regularizer, improving both finetuning and verification.

method.summary: GPT-3 models are finetuned as generators on GSM8K (with calculator annotations). A separate verifier (initialised from the generator, with a scalar value head and joint LM loss) is trained on 100 sampled completions per training problem labelled by final-answer correctness. At test time 100 completions are sampled at T=0.7 and the verifier's top-ranked one is returned.
method.task: grade school math word problems with natural-language solutions

datasets.name: GSM8K
datasets.split: 7.5K train / 1K test; training subsets of 500, 1K, 2K, 4K, 7.5K used in scaling plots
datasets.source: human problem writers (Upwork, then Surge AI); seed questions from few-shot 175B GPT-3
datasets.preprocessing: calculator annotations <<expr=result>> auto-generated by hard-coded logic and a finetuned LM

models.name: Verifier
models.params: same size as generator unless stated
models.architecture: language model with scalar head (one bias and one gain parameter on the logit of a special token), per-token value predictions
models.init_from: the corresponding finetuned generator (slightly better than pretrained LM)

training.objective: Generator: cross-entropy LM loss over training tokens (question tokens masked). Verifier: MSE value loss (per token) plus unweighted LM loss, equal mix of language and verifier data.
training.lr: Finetuning base lr alpha 1.6e-5 (3B), 1.2e-5 (6B), 1.0e-5 (12B), 6.0e-6 (175B), lr = 0.1 x alpha; verification lr 1.0e-5
training.batch_size: 3.2e4 tokens (4x for token-level verifiers in Fig 8c)
training.epochs: finetuning 20; verification: 2 for generator, 1 for verifier
training.dropout: 0.0 by default; 0.2 residual dropout in dropout experiments (after extra pretraining with dropout)
training.seeds: 3 runs (mean and std) except 175B verification single run

other.sweeps: lr and batch size swept an order of magnitude each way, no significant improvement

inference.decoding: finetuning: single argmax sample (T=0); verification: sample 100 completions, return top verifier score
inference.temperature: 0 for finetuning/test@1; 0.7 for verification samples and test@100 (1.0 negligible difference)
inference.samples: 100 completions per test problem (3200 max in Fig 7); 300 in Fig 8c

parameters.calculator: overrides sampling for tokens after '=' inside <<...>> using python eval; errors/timeouts skipped
parameters.majority vote: optionally vote among top-k ranked; optimal k 3-5 for 100 samples, ~30 for 3200

metrics.name: test solve rate
metrics.definition: percentage of test problems whose final answer is correct

metrics.name: test@N
metrics.definition: percentage of problems solved correctly at least once with N guesses

eval.protocol: Mean and std over 3 runs; 175B verification single run.

evidence.quote: Our reported test performance is therefore a slight underestimate

results.claim: 6B verification slightly outperforms a finetuned 175B model on the full training set, a boost roughly equal to a 30x model size increase.
results.setup: GSM8K full train set, 100 completions per test problem, 6B verifier+generator vs finetuned 175B
results.quote: On the full dataset, 6B veriﬁcation slightly outperforms a ﬁnetuned 175B model, thereby oﬀering a boost approximately equivalent to a 30x model size increase.

results.claim: Finetuning a 6B model to output the answer directly without steps drops accuracy drastically.
Naive log-linear extrapolation says ~10^16 parameters would be needed for 80% with finetuning.
results.setup: finetuning on full GSM8K train set, log-linear extrapolation
results.quote: a model with 1016 parameters would be required to reach an 80% solve rate

results.claim: Verifier test performance rises with completions up to 400, then declines.
results.quote: performance improves as we increase the number of completions up to 400

results.claim: Default evaluation uses 100 completions as a compute/benefit compromise.
results.quote: we evaluate veriﬁer test performance using 100 completions

results.claim: With only 100 samples the best majority-vote pool is the top 3-5 ranked; with 3200 samples about the top 30.
results.quote: approximately optimal to allow the top 30 to cast a vote

results.claim: Verification does not help at low dataset sizes; it helps once the dataset is large enough.
results.quote: it is not beneﬁcial to use veriﬁcation at low dataset sizes

results.claim: test@100 degrades sharply with more finetuning epochs while test@1 improves; generator for verifier data trained 2 epochs.
results.quote: we use models trained for 2 epochs to generate samples for training veriﬁers

results.claim: Fewer than 2 percent of GSM8K problems contain breaking errors.
results.setup: re-solve agreement check on a subset
results.quote: ﬁnding that 1.7% of problems still produce disagreements among contractors

results.claim: Fixing calculator bugs improves verification test performance by about 1% on the full train set.
results.quote: Fixing the calculator improves veriﬁcation test performance by about 1%

results.claim: Token-level verifiers outperform solution-level; larger generator matters more than larger verifier; LM joint loss helps; dropout (0.2) helps both finetuning and verification.
results.quote: We use 20% dropout for all dropout experiments

limits: Verifier labels are by final-answer correctness only, so flawed reasoning reaching the right answer gives false positives.
More search eventually finds adversarial solutions that fool the verifier.
Calculator implementation bugs make reported numbers a slight underestimate (<1% in most experiments).
Dataset may contain subtle errors beyond the 1.7% breaking-error estimate.
175B verification is a single run; absolute accuracy numbers appear only in figures.
Example solutions in Appendix D were slightly cherry-picked.

terms.definition: the percentage of problems solved correctly at least once when allowing the model to make N separate guesses for each problem
